title: Hanging pawns
line: Two pawns side by side with no pawns of their own beside them.

steps.text: Fischer against Spassky, 1972. If White takes on c5 and a pawn takes back, Black's two center pawns stand side by side alone.
Take on c5 with your pawn.
steps.after: Black takes back with a pawn.

steps.text: Two pawns side by side, with no pawn of their own on the files next to them, are hanging pawns. Tap them.
steps.hint: They stand in the middle of the board, next to each other.
steps.after: Side by side they hold the center. Only pieces can guard them.

steps.text: White castles and steps the bishop back. Black brings out its rook and knight, and the knight guards the pawn on c5.
White's plan is to attack the pawns until one has to move. The knight comes to the middle and attacks the bishop that guards d5.
Take the bishop that guards the pawn on d5.
steps.after: A pawn takes back. One guard of the pawns is gone.

steps.text: White pushes a pawn into them. Black pushes one of them ahead instead of taking.
White's pawns come forward on the right, and Black moves a rook over to the left.
The pawns no longer stand side by side. Tap the square right in front of the pawn that was left behind.
steps.hint: Black pawns move down the board. Look just below the left one of the two.
steps.after: No black pawn can attack that square now.

steps.text: Put your bishop there. No black pawn can attack it there now, and it aims at the pawn on e6 and the king behind it.
steps.after: Spassky moved his king to the corner. Fischer went on to attack it, and his attack decided the game.

summary: Hanging pawns are strong side by side. Attack them until one moves, then use the squares it leaves.
